en: Existing as an idea rather than a physical thing; not concrete
hook: ABSTRACT: pulled away (abs-tract) from the physical world.
story: Abstract. Existing as an idea rather than as a physical thing. On Memorial Day, little Leo stood with his father at the war memorial. He tugged his father's hand. "Dad, where is freedom? Can I touch it?" His father knelt beside him. "You can touch this stone, but freedom is abstract. You feel it in your heart." Abstract comes from Latin for pulled away, the same pull as in tractor: an abstract idea is pulled away from solid things. So, what word describes something like freedom or justice, which exists only as an idea? ... Abstract.

gre.s: The professor's lectures were so ____ that students begged for concrete examples, unable to connect her elegant theories to anything in the real world.
gre.clue: students begged for concrete examples

example: Mahbub found economics too abstract until a summer job at his uncle's rice mill showed him supply and demand in action.

en: Reachable or usable without difficulty; also, easy to understand
hook: ACCESSIBLE: easy ACCESS.
story: Accessible. Easy to reach or use; also, easy to understand. For two years, Natalie, who uses a wheelchair, could only look up at her university library from the bottom of its steep steps. Friends carried books down to her. This winter, a ramp and a lift were finally built. On the first morning she rolled in by herself and smiled at the shelves. The library was accessible at last. The word holds access inside it: what is accessible gives easy access. So, what word describes a place, or an idea, that is easy to reach? ... Accessible.

gre.s: Unlike his dense earlier treatises, which only specialists could follow, the philosopher's final book is remarkably ____, written in plain prose for a general audience.
gre.clue: written in plain prose for a general audience

example: Shahana's science podcast makes genetics accessible to teenagers by explaining each idea through a simple kitchen experiment.

en: A public supporter of a cause; to argue publicly in its favor
hook: ADVOCATE: in Bangladesh, a lawyer is literally called an 'advocate', someone who speaks FOR you.
story: Advocate. A person who publicly supports a cause; as a verb, to argue for it in public. Maria works in a garment factory outside the city. Every morning she watched mothers leave crying babies with neighbours. She became an advocate for a factory daycare. She collected two hundred signatures and spoke at every meeting, her voice shaking but steady. A year later, the daycare opened. Advocate shares its root with voice and vocal; in many countries, lawyers are called advocates because they speak for you. So, what do you call someone who speaks out publicly for a cause? ... Advocate.

gre.s: A longtime ____ of renewable energy, the senator surprised no one when she championed the solar subsidy bill.
gre.clue: surprised no one when she championed

example: As an advocate of cycle lanes, the young city planner rode to every council meeting on her battered bicycle.

en: Having to do with beauty and how people appreciate it
hook: AESTHETIC: think 'A STYLISH thing', all about beauty.
story: Aesthetic. Having to do with beauty and how we appreciate it. In a narrow workshop in the old city, Joe paints peacocks, rivers and film stars on rickshaw panels. A rickshaw runs just as well without them. The paintings exist for one reason: the aesthetic pleasure of everyone who watches them pass. Joe says he is giving the street something beautiful. The trick: aesthetic and anaesthetic share a Greek root about feeling; an anaesthetic stops all feeling, while aesthetic is about feeling beauty. So, what word describes anything to do with beauty and its appreciation? ... Aesthetic.

gre.s: Although the bridge is structurally sound, critics fault its ____ shortcomings, calling it the ugliest structure in the city.
gre.clue: calling it the ugliest structure in the city

example: The museum chose the old textile mill for aesthetic reasons as well as practical ones, admiring its brick arches and tall windows.

en: To stop happening or stop doing something
hook: CEASE: CEASE-FIRE, stop shooting.
story: Cease. To stop happening, or to stop doing something. For three days the monsoon rain drummed on the tin roof of Lucy's village house in the hills. Clothes would not dry, the courtyard became a pond, and the whole family stayed indoors. On the fourth morning, Lucy woke to a strange silence. The rain had ceased. She ran barefoot into the wet courtyard, [laugh] where the air smelled of mud and mango leaves. Think of a ceasefire: the moment the guns cease firing. So, what verb means to come to an end, or simply stop? ... Cease.

gre.s: The two factions agreed to ____ hostilities during the festival, but the fragile truce collapsed only days after the celebrations ended.
gre.clue: the fragile truce

example: The factory ceased production in 2019, and its empty sheds now shelter stray dogs and the occasional film crew.

en: A group of similar things close together; to gather in a group
hook: CLUSTER: like a bunch of grapes clustered together.
story: Cluster. A group of similar things close together; as a verb, to gather in a group. When the admission results went up on the notice board at the university, hundreds of students clustered around it, shoulder to shoulder, phones held high. Sam squeezed through the cluster, ran a finger down the list, and stopped at his own name. [gasp] His friends cheered, [laugh] and the cluster around him only grew. Picture lychees in June, hanging in a tight cluster from a single branch. So, what word means a tight group of similar things, or to gather into one? ... Cluster.

gre.s: Rather than being evenly distributed across the country, the new technology firms tend to ____ in a few urban centers, where investors and skilled engineers are concentrated.
gre.clue: Rather than being evenly distributed across the country

example: On cold winter mornings in Rangpur, rickshaw pullers cluster around the tea stalls, warming their hands on clay cups.

en: To invent a term or expression that did not exist before
hook: GRE trick: to COIN a word is to MINT a brand-new one, like a new coin.
story: Coin. To invent a new word or expression. One afternoon, rain began to fall while the sun was still shining. Ben's five-year-old sister pressed her face to the window and shouted, "Look, sun-rain!" The whole family laughed, but the word stuck. Now her uncles say sun-rain too, and Ben tells her proudly that she coined it. The trick: a mint stamps out a brand-new coin that passes from hand to hand, and when you coin a word, you stamp out a new one that people pass along. So, what verb means to invent a brand-new expression? ... Coin.

gre.s: Rather than borrow an existing term, the psychologist decided to ____ a new one, since no word in the language captured the phenomenon she had discovered.
gre.clue: no word in the language captured the phenomenon

example: Richard Owen, the anatomist who coined the word dinosaur, built it from Greek roots meaning terrible lizard.

en: Hard to ignore because it is so interesting or convincing
hook: COMPELLING: it COMPELS, or forces, you to pay attention.
story: Compelling. So interesting or convincing that you cannot ignore it. Alex promised himself just one chapter of a mystery novel before bed. Then the power went out, so he kept reading by the light of his phone, the fan silent. When he turned the last page, the call to dawn prayer was drifting through the window. [sigh] He had not slept at all. The story was simply too compelling. Compelling comes from compel, to force: a compelling story forces you to keep going. So, what word describes a story or argument you simply cannot put down? ... Compelling.

gre.s: Although the evidence for the hypothesis was once considered thin, the new fossil discoveries make a ____ case for it.
gre.clue: Although the evidence for the hypothesis was once considered thin

example: The defense lawyer offered a compelling alibi, backed by bus tickets and a shopkeeper who remembered serving her client that night.

en: To act according to a rule, request, or command
hook: COMPLY: COMPLETE what's asked.
story: Comply. To act according to a rule, request or command. At the GRE test centre in the city, the officer asked every candidate to remove watches, empty pockets and lock phones away. Emma complied at once and placed her things in a locker. The young man behind her argued for ten minutes about his lucky watch and nearly missed his slot. Emma sat down calm and ready. Comply comes from the same Latin root as complete: you complete, or fill out, what is asked of you. So, what verb means to follow a rule or request? ... Comply.

gre.s: Companies that refuse to ____ with the new environmental regulations will face heavy fines and possible closure.
gre.clue: will face heavy fines and possible closure

example: Passengers who refused to comply with the mask rule were politely asked to leave the train at the next station.

en: To make a problem worse
hook: GRE trick: COMPOUND interest grows; a COMPOUNDED problem grows worse.
story: Compound. To make a problem worse. Ten-year-old Danny broke his mother's favourite glass bowl, a gift from her own mother. He hid the pieces under his bed and said the cat had done it. When his mother found the pieces, it was the lie that hurt her more than the bowl. By lying, Danny had compounded his mistake. That night he confessed, and she held him close. Think of compound interest, which grows on top of itself; a compounded problem grows worse on top of itself. So, what verb means to make a bad situation even worse? ... Compound.

gre.s: The governor's initial delay in ordering an evacuation was a serious error, but her subsequent refusal to admit it served only to ____ the damage to her reputation.
gre.clue: her subsequent refusal to admit it

example: A dropped catch in the final over compounded the bowler's misery, and his team lost the match by a single run.

en: To settle differences by mutual give and take; also, to weaken or endanger
bn: আপস করা; ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত বা দুর্বল করা
hook: GRE trick: COMPROMISE also means to WEAKEN — a compromised password.
story: Compromise. To settle a disagreement by each side giving something up; also, to weaken or put at risk. Chris's parents could not agree on a winter trip. His father longed for the sea at the long sandy beach; his mother dreamed of the green tea gardens in the hills. After a long evening of debate, they reached a compromise: tea gardens this year, the sea next year. The trick: a compromise between people is healthy, but a compromised password or a compromised bridge has been weakened. So, what word means meeting halfway, with each side giving a little? ... Compromise.

gre.s: Engineers warned that cutting corners on materials would ____ the structural integrity of the bridge, putting thousands of commuters at risk.
gre.clue: putting thousands of commuters at risk

example: Sharing your password with a friend can compromise the security of every account linked to your email address.

en: Broad agreement shared by most or all members of a group
hook: CONSENSUS: everyone gives their CONSENT.
story: Consensus. Broad agreement shared by most or all of a group. In a northern village, families gathered under a huge banyan tree to decide where the new tube well should go. Some wanted it by the market, others near the mosque. Then an old woman pointed out that children walked the farthest for water, so it should stand beside the primary school. One by one, heads nodded. By sunset there was consensus. Consensus and consent share a Latin root: a consensus is when nearly everyone gives consent. So, what word means broad agreement across a whole group? ... Consensus.

gre.s: Although a few dissenters remain, the scientific ____ is that human activity is the primary driver of recent warming.
gre.clue: Although a few dissenters remain

example: After two long evenings of debate, the residents of the Mirpur building reached a consensus to paint the stairwell bright yellow.

en: A firmly held belief; also, a formal declaration of guilt
hook: CONVICTION: you're CONVINCED.
story: Conviction. A firmly held belief; also, an official ruling that someone is guilty. Fifty years ago, in a river village, Laura's grandmother decided her daughters would go to school. Neighbours whispered that girls belonged in the kitchen. She simply walked them to school every morning. Her conviction never wavered, and today two of those daughters are teachers. Conviction and convince share a Latin root: a conviction is something you are convinced of, and a court's conviction means the judge is convinced of guilt. So, what word means a belief held so firmly that nothing shakes it? ... Conviction.

gre.s: Though the young activist spoke softly, she argued with such ____ that even her skeptical audience could not doubt she believed every word.
gre.clue: could not doubt she believed every word

example: The old ferry captain told his passengers with quiet conviction that the storm would pass before they reached Barisal.

en: Cut off from something, with no real link to it
hook: GRE trick: DIVORCED FROM reality means disconnected from it.
story: Divorced. Cut off from something, with no real link to it. Josh showed his sister his new GRE timetable: twelve hours of study a day, starting at five every morning. She raised an eyebrow. "Josh, you work full time, and you have never woken up before eight." He looked again, [laugh] and laughed at himself. The plan was completely divorced from reality. The trick: a divorced couple no longer share a home, and an idea divorced from reality no longer shares anything with the real world. So, what word describes a plan cut off from real life? ... Divorced.

gre.s: Critics charged that the economist's elegant models were ____ from reality, ignoring how actual consumers behave.
gre.clue: ignoring how actual consumers behave

example: Raised in a gated compound with a driver and a cook, the diplomat's children grew up divorced from ordinary life in the city.

en: Detailed and complicated (adj.); to explain in more detail (verb)
hook: E-LABOR-ATE: lots of LABOR went into it.
story: Elaborate. As an adjective, detailed and complicated. As a verb, to explain in more detail. The night before her wedding, Isabella sat for four hours while an artist covered her hands in henna: peacocks, vines, tiny paisleys, even the groom's name hidden inside a leaf. Her cousins crowded close. "How do you plan something so elaborate?" one asked. The artist smiled and elaborated, sketching each step on paper. Inside elaborate hides labour, and its Latin source really means to work something out with effort. So, what word describes a design that is highly detailed and complex? ... Elaborate.

gre.s: Far from the simple sketch the client had requested, the architect produced a highly ____ design, crowded with ornament and dozens of interlocking spaces.
gre.clue: Far from the simple sketch the client had requested

example: The thief's elaborate plan involved a fake delivery van, two disguises, and a tunnel dug under the jeweller's back wall.

en: To give information to; also, to give an essential quality to or influence
bn: জানানো; প্রভাবিত করা, বৈশিষ্ট্য দান করা
hook: GRE trick: experience INFORMS art means it SHAPES it from within.
story: Inform. To tell someone facts; also, to shape or influence something from within. Aaron grew up on a sandbar island in a great river, where the river swallowed his family's land twice before he turned twelve. Today he is a filmmaker in the city. Every film he makes is informed by that childhood: the roar of the water, the fear of loss, the courage of starting again. His memories inform each scene he shoots. Inform literally means to give form to, so your experiences can inform your work by giving it shape. So, what verb means to shape something deeply from within? ... Inform.

gre.s: Her years as a war correspondent continue to ____ her fiction: nearly every novel she writes returns to scenes of conflict and displacement.
gre.clue: nearly every novel she writes returns to scenes of conflict and displacement

example: Her childhood among the weavers of Tangail informs every pattern the designer creates, from silk scarves to hotel carpets.

en: To suggest or hint indirectly
hook: GRE trick: as a verb, INTIMATE means to hint, like whispering an intimate secret.
story: Intimate. To suggest something indirectly; to hint. Two days before the final exam, the chemistry teacher, Miss Parker, closed her book and smiled. "I will not tell you what is on the paper. But if I were you, I would read chapter seven twice." Nobody needed more. She had intimated exactly where to look, and Rebecca spent the whole night on chapter seven. As a verb, intimate comes from the Latin for innermost: you let an inner thought slip out quietly. So, what verb means to hint at something without saying it directly? ... Intimate.

gre.s: Though she never stated it outright, the minister seemed to ____ that the government would soon change its policy.
gre.clue: Though she never stated it outright

example: The landlord intimated that the rent might rise next year, though he refused to name a figure.

en: Sharp and highly developed; eager
hook: KEEN: a KEEN knife is sharp; a keen student is eager.
story: Keen. Sharp and highly developed; also, eager. At dawn on the great river, the old fisherman Walter stood still in his boat, watching the grey water. His grandson saw nothing. Then Walter pointed to a faint silver flicker far away. "Look. Cast there." The net came up shining with fish. The boy [gasp] stared at his grandfather, amazed by his keen eyes, and became keen to learn everything he knew. The trick: a keen knife is sharp, a keen eye is sharp, and a keen student is sharp with eagerness. So, what word describes senses that are sharp and highly developed? ... Keen.

gre.s: Her ____ eye for detail made her an invaluable editor; she routinely caught errors that had slipped past three previous readers.
gre.clue: caught errors that had slipped past three previous readers

example: A keen sense of smell lets trained airport dogs detect explosives hidden inside sealed suitcases.

en: A drawback that holds someone back; also, legal responsibility for something
hook: LIABILITY: something you're LIABLE for, a burden.
story: Liability. Something that holds you back; also, legal responsibility. In his neighbourhood team in the city, Carter could hit sixes over the mango tree, but he dropped every catch that came his way. In the final, he dropped three. His captain put an arm around him. "Your bat wins matches, but in the field you are a liability. Let us practise catching." The trick: an accountant writes assets on one side and liabilities on the other; an asset lifts you up, a liability pulls you down. So, what word means a weakness that holds a person or team back? ... Liability.

gre.s: His reckless remarks to the press, once dismissed as charming, had become a serious ____ for the campaign, costing it the support of several key donors.
gre.clue: costing it the support of several key donors

example: In the summer heat, the team's ageing goalkeeper became a liability, too tired by the second half to dive for anything.

en: Humble about one's achievements; moderate in size or amount
hook: MODEST: MODERATE, not boastful, not extreme.
story: Modest. Humble about your achievements; also, moderate or small in size. When Owen came first in the board exam results, reporters crowded into his family's modest two-room house. They asked how he had done it. He looked at the floor, [chuckle] then pointed at his mother. "She woke up with me every morning. Write about her." Everyone loved how modest he was. Modest and moderate share a Latin root meaning measure: a modest person keeps praise within measure, and a modest house is of measured size. So, what word describes someone humble about success? ... Modest.

gre.s: Despite the company's grand promises of transformation, the new policy produced only ____ gains, raising productivity by barely two percent.
gre.clue: raising productivity by barely two percent

example: The bakery started with a modest budget of fifty thousand taka and one secondhand oven in a Mohammadpur garage.

en: Biased in favor of one side; also, incomplete
hook: PARTIAL: takes PART of one side, or is only a PART.
story: Partial. Biased in favour of one side; also, incomplete. At a winter rice-cake contest at their village home, Grandmother was the only judge. Her eldest grandson made perfect steamed rice cakes. Her six-year-old granddaughter made lumpy ones dripping with date molasses. Grandmother [laugh] gave first prize to the little one, who [gasp] clapped her sticky hands, and nobody was surprised. Everyone knew she was partial to her baby. The trick: a partial judge takes part with one side, while a partial payment is only part of the whole. So, what word describes a judge who favours one side? ... Partial.

gre.s: Because the judge's brother was a shareholder in the company, critics argued that she would inevitably be ____ in its favor and should withdraw from the case.
gre.clue: the judge's brother was a shareholder

example: A historian who is partial to one dynasty may quietly ignore records that show its rulers in a poor light.

en: Letting things happen without acting, reacting or resisting
hook: PASSIVE: lets everything PASS by without acting.
story: Passive. Letting things happen without acting or resisting. For a month, Luke watched GRE vocabulary videos every night, nodding along, never once testing himself. When he took a practice quiz, he could barely recall ten words. His tutor explained that passive watching feels like learning but leaves little behind. So Luke began writing sentences and quizzing himself aloud, and the words finally stuck. Picture a passive person standing still while life passes by, never reaching out to act. So, what word describes someone who just lets things happen without taking action? ... Passive.

gre.s: Far from being ____ spectators of the reforms, the village women organized committees, petitioned officials, and ultimately shaped how the new laws were enforced.
gre.clue: the village women organized committees, petitioned officials

example: A passive investor simply buys a fund that tracks the whole market and then leaves it alone for decades.

en: Obvious and clearly visible
hook: GRE trick: PATENT (adj.) means obvious — a patent lie is obvious to everyone.
story: Patent. Obvious and clearly visible. Little Noah swore he had not touched the sweets in the fridge. He said it with great seriousness, while syrup dripped from his chin and his fingers stuck together. His grandmother [chuckle] wiped his face and asked him again. It was a patent lie, plain to everyone in the room. Patent comes from the Latin for lying open, and that is also why an inventor's patent is an open public record. So, what word describes a lie so obvious that everyone can see through it? ... Patent.

gre.s: The witness's claim was ____ false, contradicted by video footage that showed him miles away at the time.
gre.clue: contradicted by video footage

example: The company's claim that its biscuits were sugar-free was a patent lie, since sugar appeared second on the ingredients list.

en: Narrow-minded and unsophisticated
hook: PROVINCIAL: from a small PROVINCE, never seen the world.
story: Provincial. Narrow-minded and unsophisticated. Henry's uncle lives in the richest part of the city and believes nothing good exists outside it. Village food is dirty, he says, and regional accents are only for jokes. Then he spent a week in Henry's mother's village far to the north. A farmer's daughter there quoted poets he had never read, and her mother cooked the best meal of his life. His views had been provincial, even though he lived in the capital. A province is a region far from the centre, and provincial thinking stays stuck in one small corner. So, what word describes narrow-minded, unworldly views? ... Provincial.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the novelist's early work as ____, concerned only with the petty gossip of her small hometown.
gre.clue: concerned only with the petty gossip of her small hometown

example: Living abroad cured Sabrina of her provincial belief that no cuisine in the world could match her mother's cooking.

en: Guided by clear thinking and good sense rather than emotion
hook: RATIONAL: uses RATIO, measured reasoning.
story: Rational. Guided by clear thinking rather than emotion. While Amy's mother was frying fish, the pan of oil suddenly caught fire. Amy's brother grabbed a jug of water, but their mother stopped him. Water would make burning oil explode. Instead, she calmly turned off the gas and slid a metal lid over the pan. The flames died at once. Her rational mind had saved the kitchen. Rational shares its Latin root with ratio and reason: a rational person reasons before acting. So, what word describes someone guided by clear thinking instead of panic? ... Rational.

gre.s: Although investors like to think of themselves as ____, studies show that their decisions are frequently driven by fear and herd behavior.
gre.clue: frequently driven by fear and herd behavior

example: Faced with a sudden fire alarm, the rational response is to leave calmly by the stairs, not to rush for the lift.

en: Firm determination; to decide firmly or settle
hook: RESOLVE: a RESOLUTION you stick to.
story: Resolve. Firm determination; as a verb, to decide firmly. As a child, Kate nearly drowned in a pond and never went near water again. At twenty-five, watching her niece splash in the river, she resolved to learn. Every dawn for two months she went to the village pond with a teacher. She swallowed water, shivered, and came back the next day. Her resolve never broke. Then one morning, she swam across. Think of a resolution you make for the new year; resolve is the strength to keep it. So, what word means firm determination to do something? ... Resolve.

gre.s: Repeated setbacks only strengthened the climbers' ____: after each failed attempt on the summit, they returned the following season eager to try again.
gre.clue: eager to try again

example: Rumana's resolve never wavered during the long rehabilitation, and she was back on the hockey field within a year of her injury.

en: Highly developed and complex; having refined, worldly taste
hook: SOPHISTICATED: from SOPHIA, wisdom; refined and advanced.
story: Sophisticated. Highly developed and complex; also, refined and worldly. Adam's grandmother pointed to a palm tree near their pond, where weaver birds hung their nests. Each one was woven from strips of grass into a hanging bottle with a long tunnel for a door, which keeps snakes out. Adam stared, amazed that a small bird could build something so sophisticated. Sophisticated comes from the Greek sophia, wisdom, which also appears in philosophy. Think of a sophisticated design as one packed with the wisdom of long experience. So, what word describes something highly developed and complex? ... Sophisticated.

gre.s: The fraud was so ____, involving dozens of shell companies across several countries, that investigators needed years to untangle it.
gre.clue: involving dozens of shell companies across several countries

example: Ancient Egyptian farmers developed a sophisticated network of canals and basins to spread the Nile's floodwater across their fields.

en: So delicate or precise as to be hard to notice or analyze
hook: SUBTLE: silent 'b', just as subtle as the word itself.
story: Subtle. So delicate or slight that it is hard to notice. Mia's uncle is a tea taster in the hills. He slurps a spoonful from a small cup, rolls it on his tongue, and says which hillside it came from and whether it was picked after rain. To Mia, every cup tastes the same. But he notices subtle differences in smell and colour that she cannot sense at all. Subtle hides a silent b, a letter so subtle that most people never notice it. So, what word describes a difference so delicate that only an expert can detect it? ... Subtle.

gre.s: The difference between the two dialects is ____, detectable only to native speakers who have lived in both regions.
gre.clue: detectable only to native speakers

example: A skilled tea taster can detect subtle differences between leaves picked in the same Sylhet garden only a week apart.

en: Completely and absolutely
hook: UTTERLY: so complete you can't UTTER anything more.
story: Utterly. Completely and absolutely. Peter took the overnight ferry from the city to reach home for the holiday. The deck was packed, the engine roared all night, and he slept sitting on his bag. When he finally reached his mother's gate at dawn, he was utterly exhausted. Then she came running out, [sigh] and he forgot every bit of it. Utter comes from an old English word for outer, so utterly means all the way to the outermost edge. So, what word means completely, to the very limit? ... Utterly.

gre.s: The expedition's plan, which had seemed flawless on paper, proved ____ unworkable: not a single stage could be carried out once the team reached the frozen pass.
gre.clue: not a single stage could be carried out

example: The old map proved utterly useless, since the river had shifted its course nearly a mile since it was drawn.

en: To produce or provide; to give way under pressure
hook: YIELD has two meanings: PRODUCE (a crop yields rice) and GIVE WAY (a yield sign).
story: Yield. To produce or provide; also, to give way under pressure. For forty years, George farmed his land near the coast the old way. When salt water crept into his fields, his daughter brought home new salt-tolerant rice seeds. He refused at first. After weeks of her patient arguing, he finally yielded. That winter his fields yielded almost twice as much rice, and he [chuckle] admitted she was right. The trick: a field yields a crop, and a yield sign on the road tells you to give way. So, what verb means both to produce and to give way? ... Yield.

gre.s: Researchers hoped the new irrigation method would ____ larger harvests, but in its first season the farms brought in less rice than ever.
gre.clue: but in its first season the farms brought in less rice than ever

example: The survey of three thousand households yielded surprising data on how much families spend on mobile phone credit.
